sources.news_title: US threatens to halt Ukraine arms
sources.text:
The US threatened to halt arms sales to Europe for use in Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian refineries, the Financial Times reported, accelerating a stunning deterioration in ties between the allies.
US President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — whom Trump called to be ousted — told Axios “was news for me.”
US threats over arms and intelligence had “ruin[ed] the trust completely,” a Ukrainian official said.
On Friday, Washington announced it would suspend sanctions on Russian diesel, though for Moscow, “the real benefit isn’t the billions of dollars in fresh revenue,” a CNN correspondent wrote. “It is the wedge this deal… drives right through the heart of the Western alliance.”

sources.news_title: TRUMP ADMINISTRATION WARNS UKRAINE: STOP HITTING RUSSIAN REFINERIES OR RISK ARMS CUTOFF
sources.text:
The United States has threatened to block arms deliveries to Ukraine over its attacks on Russian oil refineries, as the Trump administration lobbies European capitals and Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, according to a report from the Financial Times.
The warning was carried on social media by the account @FirstSquawk, which wrote that the U.S. had "threatened to block arms for Ukraine over its attacks on Russian refineries" and was "lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries." A separate post from the same account repeated that the U.S. lobbied European capitals and Kyiv to halt the attacks.
Reporting on the same subject indicates that U.S. envoys threatened to cut Ukraine's intelligence access over Russian refinery strikes, with Ukrainian officials saying that President Donald Trump's envoys raised the prospect of suspending U.S. intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued attacking Russian oil refineries. A U.S. official denies that any threat was made.
The warnings appear to follow a reported diesel deal between President Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, though the details of that arrangement have not been confirmed. The deal has not yet been confirmed by Ukraine or Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded to the pressure. Asked on "This Week" how long Ukraine can continue to defend itself as the war with Russia approaches five years, Zelenskyy said the war has to end. He also defended Ukraine's right to strike Russian oil refineries after President Trump demanded that Ukraine stop striking them.
Zelenskyy's comments came just minutes after Trump claimed an energy ceasefire had been agreed. Zelenskyy said the energy ceasefire was "news to me," according to The Independent, which reported that the deal had not been confirmed by either Ukraine or Russia.
The exchange unfolded against a backdrop of continued fighting. A Russian strike near a grocery store in Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, killed three people and injured nine, officials said. An attack on Ivano-Frankivsk in western Ukraine killed two, according to the mayor.
Meanwhile, a NATO official said Russia suffered over fifty thousand casualties in Ukraine last month, including up to twenty-eight thousand killed, compared with about five thousand Ukrainian casualties. Ukrainian forces have also recaptured over one hundred twenty-five square kilometers of territory.
The Financial Times report was amplified across social media, with the account @FirstSquawk carrying the claim in multiple posts. The same account also carried the NATO casualty figures and the reports of Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities. The Independent picked up the story, noting Zelenskyy's response to Trump's claim of an energy ceasefire. Axios, via Ukrainska Pravda, reported that U.S. envoys threatened to cut intelligence access, while a U.S. official denied any threat was made.
The posts and coverage do not provide a direct quote from the Trump administration confirming the arms block threat. The claim rests on reporting by the Financial Times and subsequent accounts. The U.S. official's denial of the intelligence threat is also reported.
Next News Network could not independently verify the claims that the United States threatened to block arms for Ukraine or that U.S. envoys threatened to cut intelligence access.
Our Take
The Trump administration is right to demand that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries. These attacks risk escalating the war and driving up global energy prices, which hurts American families. President Trump's reported diesel deal with Putin is a step toward stabilizing energy markets, but Ukraine's continued strikes undermine that effort.
Zelenskyy's defense of the strikes is predictable, but the United States cannot allow its weapons to be used in a way that provokes Russia and destabilizes global oil supplies. Cutting off arms may seem harsh, but it is a necessary lever to force Kyiv to the negotiating table. The war has to end, as Zelenskyy himself said. The American people have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on this conflict, and it is time for Europe to step up and for Ukraine to stop escalating.
The denial from a U.S. official about intelligence threats is noted, but the pattern is clear: the administration is using all available tools to rein in Ukraine's military actions. This is not about abandoning Ukraine; it is about preventing a wider war and protecting American interests. The mainstream media will frame this as a betrayal, but real leadership means making tough decisions. President Trump is doing exactly that.

FT: US Threatens to Block Arms Supplies to Ukraine Over Strikes on Russian
sources.text:
The administration of US President Donald Trump is threatening to halt sales of American weapons to Ukraine, demanding an end to strikes by the Defence Forces on Russia’s energy infrastructure.
The Financial Times reports this, citing European officials who received calls from US officials on Saturday and Sunday or were briefed on them.
The White House declined to confirm or comment on the calls.
According to FT sources, US representatives threatened to stop intelligence-sharing with Ukraine and to block the PURL mechanism — a NATO initiative under which European countries and Canada fund the purchase of US-made equipment for Ukraine
“They’re calling Kyiv... they’re calling everyone [in Europe],” said an official who was phoned by a representative of the US defence department.
Among those US representatives spoke with was Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.
As a reminder, today US President Donald Trump announced in a post on Truth Social that Ukraine and Russia had reached an agreement to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.
“In the war between Russia and Ukraine, an ENERGY CEASEFIRE takes effect immediately. Both sides have agreed. Do not violate it!” he wrote.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Russia attacked CHP-5 in Kharkiv, despite the “energy truce” announced by US President Donald Trump.
He also wrote on social media that Ukraine is ready to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop strikes on Russian refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation steps must be mutual and come with genuine guarantees,” the head of state stressed.
According to Zelenskyy, in just one week Russian forces launched about 1,450 guided aerial bombs, 75 missiles of various types and more than 1,640 attack drones at Ukraine. About 60% of the drones were jet-powered.

sources.news_title: U.S. Administration Warns Ukraine About Possible Weapon Supply Cut
sources.text:
U.S. Administration Warns Ukraine About Possible Weapon Supply Cut
Officials from the Trump administration have issued warnings to Kyiv about the potential suspension of military aid, specifically referencing the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), which allows European countries to procure U.S. weapons for Ukraine. Alongside threats to weapon support, U.S. representatives have also cautioned Ukrainian officials about the likelihood of halting intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
According to the Financial Times, U.S. officials made calls to European capitals and to Kyiv on October 10 and 11. The objective of these calls was to advocate for a cessation of Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Sources familiar with the discussions either received these calls or were informed about their contents.
One official indicated that the calls came from a representative of the U.S. Department of Defense. Among those contacted was Pavlo Palisa, Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine. The White House did not confirm or comment on these calls.
Later that day, Trump announced an energy truce between Ukraine and Russia, which both parties supposedly agreed to. In response, the Ukrainian president stated that he had no prior knowledge of such an agreement but confirmed that Ukraine would support it if Russia did as well. The Kremlin has yet to comment on this alleged agreement with Trump. However, following the announcement, Russian forces launched an attack on a thermal power plant in Kharkiv.
Context
- PURL was launched by NATO on August 4, 2025, facilitating the provision of American weaponry to Ukraine financed by European allies and Canada.
- Trump accused Kyiv of exacerbating the global diesel fuel shortage and rising prices, urging Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to reduce the intensity of attacks. Following this, on September 30, the Russian outlet “Agency” pointed out that Ukraine had supposedly ceased strikes on Russian oil refineries. However, after a brief pause, The Guardian reported on October 1 that Ukraine continued to target Russian oil facilities.
- In a Reuters interview on October 3, the Ukrainian president claimed that Ukraine would intensify strikes on Russian oil refineries in retaliation for Russia’s increased attacks on civilian infrastructure, asserting that the Kremlin aims to force residents of Kyiv and other cities to leave before winter. Zelensky emphasized that Ukraine’s response would not target civilian populations.
- On October 9, Trump held a phone call with illegitimate Russian President Vladimir Putin, following which he announced an agreement for the supply of Russian diesel to the U.S. and global markets. According to a temporary general license from OFAC, the permission will remain valid until April 7, 2027.
- Financial Times, citing sources on October 10, reported that following Trump’s easing of sanctions on Russian diesel, officials in his administration intensified pressure on Ukraine to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries, threatening to halt intelligence sharing with Ukraine if they refused. During this meeting, the Ukrainian negotiating team learned of Trump’s decisions and the easing of sanctions on Russian diesel, resulting in the negotiations being shortened from two days to one.
